clinicalScope: Acute traumatic bone fractures in children and adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Bone Fractures
subject: Medicine
summary: A fracture is a break in bone that causes pain, swelling and loss of function. In low‑resource settings the clinician must rely on history, physical exam and plain radiography, while planning safe immobilisation and infection prevention.

sections.p: A fracture is a disruption of the continuity of bone cortex, with or without displacement, that may be closed or open.
b: Globally, trauma accounts for >90 % of fractures; in East Africa road‑traffic injuries and falls are the leading mechanisms.
Children have a higher proportion of green‑stick and buckle fractures; adults over 60 y have more osteoporotic hip fractures.
Open (compound) fractures occur in 5‑10 % of all fractures and carry a high infection risk in settings with limited sterile supplies.
Seasonal peaks correspond to agricultural work (wet season) and school sports (dry season).

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Most fractures result from mechanical forces that exceed bone strength.
b: High‑energy blunt trauma – road‑traffic collisions, falls from height >1 m.
Low‑energy falls in the elderly with osteoporosis or vitamin D deficiency.
Pathological bone weakened by chronic infection (osteomyelitis), sickle‑cell disease, or metastatic cancer.
Repetitive stress in athletes or laborers (stress fractures).
Malnutrition, chronic steroid use, and HIV‑associated bone loss increase susceptibility.

sections.p: Fracture occurs when applied force surpasses the elastic limit of bone, causing micro‑cracks that coalesce into a complete break.
b: Immediate mechanical disruption leads to hemorrhage, periosteal stripping and release of inflammatory mediators.
Hematoma formation initiates the inflammatory phase, recruiting neutrophils and macrophages.
Soft callus (fibro‑cartilage) forms within 1‑2 weeks, providing provisional stability.
Hard callus (woven bone) replaces soft callus by 3‑6 weeks; remodeling to lamellar bone continues for months.
In open fractures, bacterial contamination can convert the normal healing cascade into chronic osteomyelitis.

sections.p: Patients typically notice sudden, severe pain at the injury site with functional loss.
b: Localized tenderness, swelling and bruising.
Visible deformity or shortening of the limb.
Crepitus – a grating sensation felt when the fragments move.
Inability to bear weight (lower limb) or use the limb (upper limb).
Open fracture: bone protruding through skin, active bleeding, contamination.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused trauma history combined with a systematic neuro‑vascular exam guides urgent management.
b: Mechanism of injury – height, speed, object, point of impact.
Time since injury, prior fractures, osteoporosis risk factors, HIV/TB status.
Pain severity, ability to move, numbness or tingling distal to the site.
Inspect for open wound, contamination, distal pulses, capillary refill, motor and sensory function.
Check for compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic fracture must be excluded to avoid missed injuries.
b: Severe sprain or ligament tear – pain but no bony deformity; intact neuro‑vascular exam.
Contusion with soft‑tissue hematoma – swelling without cortical disruption on imaging.
Dislocation – loss of joint congruity without fracture line; may coexist.
Acute osteomyelitis – localized pain, fever, but no acute trauma history.
Bone tumor (e.g., osteosarcoma) presenting with pathologic fracture – history of progressive pain before injury.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: In low‑resource settings plain radiography is the cornerstone; adjuncts are used when available.

t.b: Confirms fracture line, displacement, comminution, and detects open fracture fragments.

t.a: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
t.b: Detects intra‑abdominal bleeding in pelvic or femur fractures.
Screen for infection in open fractures; elevated WBC/ESR suggest osteomyelitis.
Identifies hypoglycaemia that can mimic altered mental status in severe trauma.

sections.p: Fractures are classified by location, pattern and soft‑tissue involvement.
b: Gustilo‑Anderson classification for open fractures (Type I‑III) guides antibiotic choice and timing of debridement.
AO/OTA system categorises fracture morphology (simple, wedge, complex) and guides fixation strategy.
Compartment syndrome is staged by pressure (>30 mmHg) or clinical criteria; requires emergent fasciotomy.
Polytrauma (Injury Severity Score ≥ 16) mandates whole‑body assessment and possible damage‑control orthopaedics.

sections.p: Local and systemic factors can impede healing or mask severity.
b: Malnutrition, vitamin D deficiency, and chronic HIV infection delay callus formation.
Concurrent malaria or severe anaemia reduces oxygen delivery to the fracture site.
Traditional bone‑setting practices may introduce infection or cause mal‑alignment.
Concurrent anticoagulant therapy (e.g., warfarin) increases risk of hematoma expansion.
Delayed presentation (>24 h) raises infection risk in open fractures.

sections.p: Initial care focuses on stabilisation, analgesia, infection control and definitive fixation.
b: 1️⃣ Primary survey – airway, breathing, circulation; control external bleeding.
2️⃣ Analgesia – paracetamol ± NSAID; opioid rescue if pain uncontrolled.
3️⃣ Immobilisation – splint or traction; maintain alignment, avoid further displacement.
4️⃣ Open fracture – give first‑generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefazolin) within 1 h; consider metronidazole if contaminated.
5️⃣ Tetanus prophylaxis – booster if >5 y since last dose.
6️⃣ Definitive fixation – casting for simple closed fractures; surgical fixation (intramedullary nail, plate) for displaced or unstable fractures when theatre is available.
7️⃣ Post‑operative monitoring – neuro‑vascular checks every 2 h for 24 h, wound inspection, pain control.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications prevents morbidity and mortality.
b: Compartment syndrome – pain out of proportion, pallor, pulselessness; requires emergent fasciotomy.
Neuro‑vascular injury – loss of distal pulses or motor function; urgent reduction or vascular repair.
Infection – increasing pain, purulent discharge, fever; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics and debride.
Non‑union – persistent pain and lack of callus at 3 months; consider bone grafting.
Fat embolism syndrome – respiratory distress, petechial rash, altered mental status after long‑bone fracture.
Children – prefer closed reduction and casting; avoid growth‑plate injury.
Elderly with osteoporosis – consider surgical fixation to allow early mobilisation.
Pregnant women – protect fetus from radiation; use shielding and limit X‑ray to essential views.
Patients with sickle‑cell disease – aggressive pain control, hydration, and infection prophylaxis.
HIV‑positive patients – monitor CD4 count; treat opportunistic infections before elective surgery.

sections.p: Healing time varies; functional outcome depends on timely care and rehabilitation.
b: Typical radiographic union: 6‑8 weeks for long bones, 3‑4 weeks for ribs.
Early physiotherapy reduces stiffness and improves return to work.
Fall‑prevention programmes (home safety, vision correction) lower hip fracture incidence in the elderly.
Calcium + vitamin D supplementation and weight‑bearing exercise improve bone density.
Community education on safe traditional bone‑setting reduces infection rates.

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls are common in low‑resource environments.
b: Normal X‑ray does not exclude occult fracture; consider repeat imaging or ultrasound if pain persists.
Absence of fever does not rule out infection in immunocompromised patients.
Peripheral pulses may be palpable despite compartment syndrome; rely on pain and tense swelling.
Elevated ESR may be due to malaria; correlate clinically before labeling osteomyelitis.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe uncontrolled pain, loss of distal pulses, or expanding swelling (suspect compartment syndrome).
Visible bone protruding through skin with heavy contamination.
Signs of systemic infection: fever >38 °C, tachycardia, hypotension.
Neurological deficit distal to the fracture.

faq.q: Can a fracture heal without a cast?
faq.a: Minor, non‑displaced fractures may unite with splinting and protected weight‑bearing, but most need immobilisation to ensure proper alignment.

faq.q: Why are antibiotics given before surgery for an open fracture?
faq.a: Early antibiotics reduce bacterial load and lower the risk of osteomyelitis; timing within 1 hour is critical.

faq.q: Is it safe to give NSAIDs for fracture pain?
faq.a: Short‑term NSAIDs provide analgesia and do not significantly impair bone healing; avoid prolonged use in patients with renal disease.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents after a fall from a mango tree with a mid‑shaft tibial fracture and a swollen calf; what is your next immediate step and why? — Perform neuro‑vascular assessment and check for compartment syndrome before splinting.

Explain how the Gustilo‑Anderson classification influences antibiotic choice in open fractures. — Type I: cefazolin alone; Type II: cefazolin + metronidazole; Type III: broad‑spectrum coverage, consider gram‑negative agents.

A child has a green‑stick fracture of the radius; why is closed reduction preferred over surgical fixation? — The periosteum remains intact, allowing rapid remodeling without disturbing growth plates.
What clinical signs differentiate compartment syndrome from a simple painful fracture? — Pain on passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia, and pain out of proportion to injury.
In an elderly patient with a hip fracture, what factor most strongly predicts mortality? — Pre‑existing frailty and delayed surgery (>48 h).

How does HIV infection alter fracture healing and what management adjustments are needed? — Delayed callus formation; ensure optimal nutrition, control opportunistic infections, and monitor for delayed union.

A patient with a femoral shaft fracture develops sudden dyspnoea, petechial rash and confusion; what is the likely complication and immediate management? — Fat embolism syndrome; provide oxygen, supportive care, and consider ICU admission.
Why is tetanus prophylaxis mandatory in open fractures even if the patient reports recent vaccination? — Wound contamination can reactivate dormant spores; booster needed if >5 y since last dose.
Describe the radiographic features that distinguish a comminuted fracture from a simple transverse fracture. — Multiple fracture fragments and loss of cortical continuity versus a single clean line.

What are the indications for damage‑control orthopaedics in polytrauma patients? — Hemodynamic instability, severe chest/abdominal injury, and need to limit operative time to prevent the ‘second hit’.
